dataset.name: Oceanographic Conditions. 2007 - 2040. North Slope Alaska.
description: Complete representations of oceanographic conditions require spatial and temporal information about the significant wave height (Hs), peak wave period (Tp), wind speed, wind direction, wave direction, water level, salinity, and temperature. This data develops location-independent typologies to reduce the number of boundary conditions needed to assess nearshore oceanographic environments in both a Historical (2007-2019) and Future (2020-2040) timespan along the Alaskan North Slope. Wave information for both time spans were generated from WaveWatch III, Delft3D-FLOW, and Delft3D-WAVE simulations forced by wind conditions from reanalysis data (e.g., ASRv2 and ERA5) for the historical simulations while projected conditions were obtained from downscaled GFDL-CM3 forced under RCP8.5 conditions. Salinity was generated from GOFS 3.1 for the years between 2008-2015 and skin temperature of the ocean was obtained from ASRv2 reanalysis data for the years between 2007-2016. To identify generalized oceanographic typologies, K-means clustering was applied to the energy-weighted joint-probability distribution of Hs and Tp at six sites along the North Slope of Alaska. Distributions of wave and wind direction, wind speed, and water level associated with locaiton-indepndent centroids were assigned single values to describe a reduced order, typological rendition of offshore oceanographic conditions. These final typologies and their constituent data are provided here and can be used to evaluate the change in ocean energy over the next two decades in response to climate change and provide insight into expected consequences such as coastal erosion and flooding. A full assessment of the findings and techniques developed can be found in:

Eymold, W.K., Flanary, C., Erikson, L., Nederhoff, K., Chartrand, C.C., Jones, C., Kasper, J., and Bull, D.L. Typological Representation of the Offshore Oceanographic Environment along the Alaskan North Slope. Continental Shelf Research (2022). 10.1016/j.csr.2022.104795

measurementTechnique:
For each site, a .MAT file is provided which contains the timeseries data in an hourly format for the historical (July-Nov 2007-2019) and future (June-Dec 2020-2040) timespans that describe the significant wave height, peak wave period, wind speed, wind direction, wave direction, and water level associated with each site. Additionally, each point in time was assigned to a specific cluster based on K-means clustering of the Hs-Tp pairs. These memberships are also included to allow for deeper analysis of each cluster or selection of different modal peaks from the variable distributions. Scripts used to calculate the JPDs and to cluster Hs and Tp at each site are included as well. The temperature and salinity profiles for each site and the average profile for each variable is available in salinity.mat. A full methodology can be found in: Eymold, W.K., Flanary, C., Erikson, L., Nederhoff, K., Chartrand, C.C., Jones, C., Kasper, J., and Bull, D.L. Typological Representation of the Offshore Oceanographic Environment along the Alaskan North Slope. Continental Shelf Research (2022). 10.1016/j.csr.2022.104795. An abbreviated version is detailed below.
Experimental design, materials and methods
Time series data were collected and combined to form CSV files for each station and year. These were converted to .MAT format (csv2mat.m) containing all years in the timespan and stored with the timespan and site name in the title. Ultimately, joint-probability distributions (JPD) were calculated for each site in the given timespan and stored as .MAT files (mat2JPD.m) for subsequent processing and visualization. The k-means clustering routine was applied to each of the JPDs to determine the location-dependent clusters associated with each site (locationKmeans.m) and the membership of each point in time for the other variables (e.g., wave direction, wind speed, wind direction, water level). The average annual power flux (AAP) (kW/m) represents the average energy delivered in a year for a given spectral shape and is given by:
AAP=\ \sum{JPD\left(H_s,T_p\right)\ast J(H_s,T_p)}=\ \sum_{ij}{{JPD}_{ij}\ast J_{ij}} (Equation 1)
where the power flux Jij (kW/m) for each sea state is given by:
J\left(H_s,T_p\right)=J_{ij}=\ \sum_{f}{\rho g c_{g,f}S_{ij}\left(\omega_f\right)\Delta\omega_f} (Equation 2),
and where ρ is the density of water, g is gravity, ij to the specific sea state (Hs,Tp pair), and cg,f is the group velocity obtained through the dispersion relationship (see Holthuijsen (2010) for more information regarding linear wave theory). We used the standard Joint North Sea Wave Observation Project (JONSWAP) spectral shape with a γ value of 3.3 to calculate AAP at each of the sites. The energy-weighted occurrence, ζij, scales each occurrence value, JPDij, by the energy in that sea-state, Jij, and is then normalized by the AAP:
\zeta_{ij}=\ \frac{{JPD}_{ij}\ \times\ J_{ij}\ }{AAP} or \zeta_{ij}=\ \frac{\ {JPD}_{ij}\ \times\ J_{ij}}{\sum_{ij}{{JPD}_{ij}J_{ij}}} (Equation 3).
K-means clustering of the energy-weighted occurrence of Hs and Tp was run at each site using the kmeans.m function of MATLAB to choose k different representations of the energy-weighted occurrence diagram that minimizes within cluster variances. An initial set of k pairs of Hs-Tp values are selected uniformly at random from the full set of energy-weighted occurrence JPD values at a given site. The squared Euclidean distances, SEDik, between these k pairs and the pairs from each sample i in the JPD are calculated as:
SED_{ik}=\ \sqrt[2]{{{(H}_{si}-\ H_{sk})}^2+\ {{(T}_{pi}-\ T_{pk})}^2} (Equation 4),
where Hsk and Tpk are the centroid values for significant wave height and peak period for the kth cluster and Hsi and Tpi are the significant wave height and peak period values for the ith point in the JPD for a specific site. Each point in the JPD is then assigned as a member of the centroid for which this distance, SEDik, is minimized. After the distances and assignments are determined, updated centroid clusters (Hsk and Tpk) are recalculated by taking the average Hs and Tp values from all members of each cluster and the distance and assignment calculations are repeated. The total squared Euclidean distance, SEDK, is the objective function of the algorithm determined as the sum of all K of the individual cluster distances for only their respective members:
S{ED}_K=\ \sum_{1}^{K}\min{{SED}_{ik}} (Equation 5),
where the minimum SEDik is used to assign sample i to cluster k. The k-means clustering process continues until SEDK no longer decreases when the new centroids are calculated. This process was conducted for 100 iterations with a different set of randomly selected starting Hs-Tp centroids each time. The final outputs of the algorithm are the Hs and Tp values for each centroid cluster, as well as the identification number (1 through k) that is used to assign each pair as a member of the centroid with the lowest squared Euclidean distance.
The individual centroids from all sites were sorted by increasing Tp value and then averaged together to calculate the preliminary centroid pool for the six Location-Independent clusters. These average values are then adjusted to select values that plot along lines of constant inverse steepness, a ratio of the wavelength based on Tp (λTp) and water depth to Hs. As informed by Location-Dependent centroids, these target inverse steepness values (with increasing Tp value) are 35-40-60-40-60-50 for the Historical data, and for the Future data they are 35-40-50-45-50-40. The average Tp values are rounded and the Hs is adjusted until the centroid lies upon the targeted constant steepness curve. These adjusted parameters are the Location-Independent centroid values. Once the Location-Independent centroids are determined, we then calculate membership to those centroids for each location. In this final clustering step each location’s Hs-Tp pair is reclassified using the values of SEDik based on the distance from the Location-Independent centroids calculated to establish the final cluster memberships for each centroid. Since the centroids do not represent the minimum distance calculation, the final SEDK calculation for each site will yield a higher value than those from the Location-Dependent clustering conducted initially.
The memberships of the Location-Dependent Hs and Tp pairs are temporally associated with additional oceanographic and atmospheric data needed to establish the boundary conditions for nearshore modeling. For each Location-Independent centroid, the distributions of wave direction, water level, wind speed, and wind direction at each site were evaluated to determine a representative value for each parameter. For each site in the study area, we determined the shoreline orientation at the nearest onshore location. The wave and wind orientations from every site were rotated by the angle perpendicular to the shoreline so that the coastline runs along a horizontal direction in map view. The rotated wave and wind data at each site were then evaluated to assess the distributions across the full study area. Distributions of each associated parameter were plotted for all sites and we determined a single value for the wave direction, wind direction, wind speed, and water level based on the modal peak of these distributions. We define the modal peak as the parameter value with the highest normalized value based on distribution profiles at the six analysis sites.
We collected GOFS 3.1 salinity data for the six sites between 2008-2015 and determined the average profile from July 1 to November 28 at each site. We then took the mean of these six average profiles to calculate a representative salinity profile for the entire coastline. From this representative profile, we calculated the ice-free season average (μs) and standard deviation (σs) for the Arctic Ocean salinity. The Historical salinity value was then set to μs and because salinity data were unavailable for the Future timespan, the Future value was set to μs – σs, reflecting the expected decrease in salinity as Arctic ice melts in the future. The process was repeated for temperature where we calculated average profiles using the ASRv2 skin temperature data at the nearest location to each site for the years 2007-2016. To select a single temperature value to represent the Arctic Ocean for both timespans, we calculated the average temperature (μT) and standard deviation (σT) from a 72-hour window in late summer (August 27-29) and set the Historical value to μT. Although sea surface temperatures are available for GFDL-CM3, the SNAP downscaling process was not optimized to account for sea surface temperatures. Thus, similar to salinity, Future values were simplistically set to μT + σT to reflect the expected increase in Arctic temperatures during 2020-2040.
